sentences.text: This petition under Section 166 MV Act is filed by the Petitioner seeking compensation of Rs.30,00,000/- for the injuries sustained in a road traffic accident.

2. It is the specific case of the petitioner that on 04-08-2022 at about 10.30 a.m., while he was travelling in a car bearing Reg. No. No.KA-04-MD-9162 along with his friends from Kudur on Kunigal-Tumkur road, near Aishwarya Layout, Narughalli Katte, Konnudike handpost to Kudur road, Tumkur taluk and district.
the lorry bearing Reg. No. KA-06-AA-0985 (hereinafter referred to as the offending vehicle) came in a rash and negligent manner and collided against the car.

As a result, the petitioner sustained grievous injuries and was treated in Aditya Hospital, Tumakuru,
then shifted to Sanjay Gandhi Hospital, Bengaluru and later to Sri Rama Hospital, Bengaluru, where he was treated as an inpatient and underwent surgery.
He has asserted that he has incurred an expenditure of about Rs. 2,00,000/- towards medical expenses and other incidental charges.

The petitioner further contends that at the time of accident he was a student of engineering and aged about 20 years, also engaged in business earning Rs. 30,000/- per month, and due to the accident he lost concentration in studies, lost prospective career and income.
On these grounds, he claims a total compensation of Rs. 30,00,000/- from the respondents.

3. In response, Respondent No. 1 (owner of the lorry) has filed written statement denying negligence on the part of the lorry driver and instead contending that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the car driver Manoj K., who is also the RC owner of the said car.
It is also contended that the petition is bad for non-joinder of necessary parties since the owner and insurer of the car were not impleaded.
Respondent No. 1 further states that the lorry was duly insured at the time of accident, and on this ground prayed for dismissal of the petition.
4. Respondent No. 2 (insurer of the lorry) has admitted that a policy was issued covering the offending vehicle and the same was in force on the date of accident.
However, it is pleaded that liability is always subject to terms and conditions of the policy.
The insurer has denied negligence on the part of the lorry driver and contended that the lorry driver did not possess a valid driving licence as on the date of accident.
It is also contended that the accident occurred entirely due to rash and negligent driving of the car driver.
Respondent No. 2 further contends that the petition suffers from non-joinder of necessary parties, since the owner and insurer of the car were not impleaded.
It is also pleaded that mandatory provisions under Section 134(c) and Section 158(6) of the MV Act were not complied with either by the owner of the lorry or the police.
It is further contended that the offending vehicle did not have a valid fitness certificate and permit as on the date of accident.
The insurer has also denied the nature of injuries, treatment, and expenses claimed, terming the compensation as excessive and exaggerated.

On the basis of the above pleadings, the following issues have been framed :-
1.Whether the petitioner proves that he sustained injuries when he was travelling in Car bearing No.KA-04-MD- 9162 on 04-08-2022 about 10.30 a.m. near Iswarya Layout, Naruganahalli Katte, Honnudike hand post to Kudur road, Tumkur District, only due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of the Lorry bearing No.KA-06-AA-0985?
2.
What compensation petitioner is entitled?
3. W hat order ?
6. In order to prove the claim, the Petitioner examined himself as PW.1 and in support of his case, 3 witnesses were examined as PW-2 to 4 and got marked the documents as per Ex.P.1 to P.21.
On the other hand the Respondent No.1 got examined one of its Directors as RW.1 and got marked 2 documents as per Ex.R1 and 2.

Respondent No.2 has examined its official as RW-2 and got marked the documents at Ex.R.3 to 7.
7.
I have heard the arguments of counsel for the Petitioner and respondents and have perused the material on record.

8. My findings to the above issues are as under:
Issue No.1: In the Affirmative. Issue No.2: Partly in the Affirmative.

Issue No.3: As per the final order, for the following:
REASONS 9. ISSUE NO.1:-

The case of the petitioner is that on 04-08-2022 at about 10.30 a.m., while he was travelling in a car bearing Reg. No. No.KA-04-MD-9162 along with his friends from Kudur on Kunigal-Tumkur road, near Aishwarya Layout, Narughalli Katte, Konnudike handpost to Kudur road, Tumkur taluk and district.
The offending vehicle came in a rash and negligent manner and collided against the car.
As a result, the petitioner sustained grievous injuries.

10. In order to prove his case, the petitioner has filed the affidavit under order XVIII rule 4 of CPC in lieu of examination in chief and examined as PW1 and he has reiterated the averments of the petition and has produced the police records at Ex. P1 to P6.
These include the FIR, complaint, spot mahazar, wound certificate, IMV report, and charge sheet.

These documents, when read together,
establish that the accident occurred on 04-08-2022 at about 10.30 a.m. near the place of occurrence, and that the petitioner sustained injuries in the said accident.
11. To further strengthen his case, the petitioner examined the Front Office Executive of Ram Hospital as PW2, who produced the hospital documents at Ex.P14 and P15.

The petitioner also Praveen G.R vs Vahini Irrigation Pvt Ltd on 6 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/161438824/
3 examined Dr. C.V. Kumar, Orthopedic Surgeon, as PW3, who produced the treatment records at Ex.
P16 and P17.

sentences.text: Most importantly, the driver of the car, who was also an eyewitness, was examined as PW4, and he categorically deposed that the lorry came in high speed from the opposite direction and dashed against the car.
He further clarified that due to the impact, the petitioner and other inmates of the car sustained grievous injuries.
12. As per Exhibit P4, Wound Certificate, the petitioner sustained fracture of both bones of the left leg and fracture of the fifth metatarsal bone.
The doctor has opined that the injuries were grievous in nature.
13. On the contrary, Respondent No.1 (owner of the lorry) did not deny the occurrence of the accident or the fact that the petitioner sustained injuries.
His specific case, however, was that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving by the driver of the car, and not on the part of the lorry driver.
14. Respondent No.2 (insurer of the lorry) took a stronger stand, disputing the very involvement of the lorry in the accident.

It was contended that the petitioner, in active collusion with the police,
created false documents only to implicate the lorry and claim compensation.
Reliance was placed on the Wound Certificate and Discharge Summary, where the history of injury was recorded as "self-fall."

On that basis, it was argued that the injuries were not the result of a motor accident but due to a fall.
15.

To support their defence, RW1 (Director of Respondent No.1) reiterated that the lorry was being driven slowly on the left side of the road, whereas the car came in a rash and negligent manner and dashed against the lorry.
RW2 (official of the insurer) also reiterated the insurer's written statement and produced Exhibits R5 to R7, which noted the history as self-fall and absence of MLC intimation.
16. PW-1 was cross-examined at length by the learned counsel for Respondent No.1.
It is significant to note that Respondent No.1 did not dispute the involvement of the offending vehicle in the accident.

The only suggestion put forth was that the accident occurred due to the negligence of the car driver and not on the part of the lorry driver, which was specifically denied by PW-1.
17.
During cross-examination by the learned counsel for Respondent No.2, PW-1 was confronted with Exhibit P-4 (Wound Certificate), wherein the history was recorded as "self-fall."
PW-1 admitted that such an entry existed.
It was further suggested to him that had he worn a seat belt, he would not have sustained the said injuries.
These suggestions were denied.
18. PW-4, the eyewitness and driver of the car, was also cross-
examined at length by Respondent No.1.
Here again, the involvement of the offending vehicle was not disputed.
The sole suggestion was that the accident was caused by the rash and negligent driving of the car driver, which PW-4 categorically denied.
Even during the cross-examination by Respondent No.2, PW-4 adhered to his version that the lorry driver was negligent and caused the accident.

sentences.text: Thus, the cross-examination of PW-1 and PW- 4 does not shake their credibility.

On the contrary, it reinforces that Respondent No.1 admits the involvement of the vehicle but shifts the blame onto the car driver, while Respondent No.2 attempts to rely solely on the medical records showing "self-fall," which by themselves cannot outweigh the consistent oral and documentary evidence on record.
20. It is pertinent to note that Respondent No.1 has not disputed the accident and the injuries sustained by the petitioner is highly material.
Once the owner of the lorry admits the involvement of his vehicle, the insurer cannot successfully argue that the vehicle was not involved.
The stand of Respondent No.2 that the lorry was falsely implicated cannot override the admission of Respondent No.1.
21. The history of "self-fall" recorded in the Wound Certificate and Discharge Summary.

It is a well-established principle that the history in medical documents is often based on information given by the patient or attendants at the time of admission, and the primary duty of the doctor is treatment, not investigation of the cause of accident.
Thus, such entries by themselves cannot discredit the police records and the consistent version of eyewitnesses.
22. The FIR, complaint, spot mahazar, IMV report, and charge sheet (Ex P1 to P6) are official records prepared in the normal course of investigation.
They clearly establish that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the lorry.
Significantly, Respondent No.2 has not challenged the charge sheet before any competent court, nor has it produced any contrary investigation report.
Hence, the contention that the lorry was falsely implicated remains an unsubstantiated allegation.
23. Though there was a one-day delay in lodging the complaint, this Tribunal is of the view that such delay is not fatal.
The petitioner was under medical treatment, and delay of one day is natural in such circumstances.
Minor delay cannot outweigh otherwise consistent and corroborated evidence.
24. The testimony of PW1 and PW4 is consistent, reliable, and corroborated by the police records.
Nothing substantial has been elicited in cross- examination to discredit them.

On the other hand,
the suggestion of self-fall is supported only by an entry in the medical records, which cannot prevail over strong oral and documentary evidence supported by an admitted accident.
25. Respondent No. 2 has not produced any credible evidence to rebut the charge sheet or substantiate the plea of false implication.
involving allegations of collusion or false implication is misplaced,
In the present matter, no cogent material produced to support the plea of collusion.
If indeed collusion existed, Respondent No. 2 ought to have initiated appropriate proceedings before the Investigating Authorities or Court, which has not been done.
Mere allegations unsupported by proof cannot be accepted.
26. In motor accident claims, the standard of proof is not beyond reasonable doubt, but on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.

Applying these principles, the case of the petitioner stands fortified by both oral and documentary evidence, while the Respondent's defence remains Praveen G.R vs Vahini Irrigation Pvt Ltd on 6 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/161438824/

sentences.text: 27. From the above discussion, I hold that the accident occurred solely due to rash and negligent driving by the driver of the offending vehicle, resulting in grievous injuries to the petitioner.

Hence,
Issue No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.
28. ISSUE NO.2 :- Due to the accident the petitioner has sustained grievous injuries.
He was immediately taken to Aidtya Hospital, Tumkur, after first aid, he was shifted to Sanjaygandhi hospital, Bengaluru, then admitted to Sri Rama hospital, Bengaluru, wherein he underwent surgery.

29. PW-3, Dr. C.V. Kumar, Orthopedic Surgeon, has deposed that the petitioner sustained a fracture of both bones of the left leg and a fracture of the right fifth metatarsal, for which he was operated upon at Sriram Hospital.
Further, on 04-01-2024, he examined the petitioner for the purpose of disability assessment.

At the time of examination, the petitioner complained of pain and swelling over the left leg and right foot, as well as difficulty in squatting, sitting cross-legged, climbing stairs,
and running.
30.
PW-3 has further stated that the fractures had united and the implants were removed.

On examination, he assessed the disability of the left lower limb at 36%, the disability of the right lower limb at 3%, and the overall disability of the whole body at 13%.
31.

It is pertinent to note that while PW-3 has made an assessment of the permanent physical disability of the limbs and the whole body, there is no specific opinion regarding the functional disability, i.e., how far the injuries affect the earning capacity and day-to-day functioning of the petitioner.
32. Moreover, the petitioner has asserted that he was a student and simultaneously doing business.
However, he has not produced any documentary evidence either to show discontinuation of his studies or to substantiate his claim of doing business.
Hence, there is no reliable material to establish how exactly the injuries have affected his earning capacity or educational career.

33. Therefore, while the medical assessment of 13% whole body disability has been placed on record,
this Tribunal is of the view that the said percentage appears to be on the higher side, considering the nature and location of injuries, the healing of fractures, and the petitioner's ability to perform normal daily activities.
Taking into account the medical evidence and the overall circumstances, this Tribunal reasonably assesses the functional disability at 10% to the whole body, which would meet the ends of justice.
34. In the petition the age of the petitioner is mentioned as 20 years.

Ex.P.11 - Aadhar card of the petitioner shows that he was born on 03-05-2003, the same is considered, then age of the petitioner as on the date of accident as 19 years and the multiplier applicable to the case on hand is 18.
35.
At time of the accident, the petitioner was 19 years old and student and also doing business in part time and earning Rs.30,000/-p.m.
It is asserted that he has lost his academic year.

2However, the petitioner has not produced any documents to substantiate his income.
In the absence of proof of income, this tribunal is of the opinion that the notional income to be assessed as per the guidelines of the Karnataka State Legal Service Authority.
Since the accident has been occurred in the year 2022, notional income Rs.15,500/- per month is taken for the assessment of compensation.

36. Thus this tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner who sustained the injuries is entitled for compensation under the following heads:
37. Loss of future income on account of permanent disability:

Considering the petitioner's grievous injury which has resulted in difficulty in mobility and in performing daily vocational activities, this court is of the opinion that the functional disability of 10% is reasonable and just.
The petitioner was 19 years old as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 18.
The notional income taken as Rs 15,500 x 12 x 18 x 10/100= Rs.3,34,800 /- towards loss of future income.
38. Pain and sufferings:

So far as the compensation under non-pecuniary damages are concerned,
considering the nature of the injury, which has resulted in difficulty in mobility and in performing daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of inpatient treatment and physical and mental suffering endured by the petitioner, this tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of .40,000/-
would be just and fair compensation under the head pain and sufferings.
39. Loss of amenities of life: undoubtedly the petitioner is suffering from difficulties in performing day to day activities and is facing continuous hardship due to the disability.
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .30,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
40. Medical expenses:
Under the pecuniary damages, expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization and medicines, the Petitioner has relied on medical bills at Ex.P.10.
On perusal of these medical bills, it reveals that the Petitioner has spent .1,21,849/- towards medical expenses.
The medical bills appears to be genuine.

Therefore, the Petitioner is entitled for medical expenses of .1,21,849/-
towards Medical Expenses.
41. Conveyance, food and nourishment charges:

Ex.P.7 -Discharge summary show that Petitioner was treated as an inpatient at Sri Rama Hospital, Bengaluru, from 04-08-2022 to 06-08-2022 and Ex.P.8 -Discharge summary show that Petitioner was treated as an inpatient at True Life Speciality Hospital, Bengaluru, from 28-01-2023 to 29-01-2023 i.e, totally for a period of 5 days.

Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award compensation of .5,000/-
under the head of conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges.
42. Loss of earning during laid up period:

With regard to the loss of earnings during treatment period, Considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in significant difficulty in mobility and in carrying out daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of impatient Praveen G.R vs Vahini Irrigation Pvt Ltd on 6 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/161438824/
7 treatment and recovery, this tribunal considers the 3 months for rest is considered .

44. Liability:
Respondent No.1 being the owner and the Respondent No.2 being the insurer of the offending vehicle are jointly and severally liable to pay the above compensation.

However,
Respondent No.2 is liable to pay compensation to the Petitioner with interest at 6% p.a.
With these observation I answer Issue No.2 partly in the affirmative.
45. ISSUE NO.3 :

In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to above Issues,
I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER Claim Petition filed under Sec.166 of M.V.Act is allowed in part with cost.

Petitioner is awarded compensation of Rs.5,78,149/- together with interest @ 6% p.a.
from the date of petition till the date of deposit with the Tribunal.
Respondent No.2 shall pay the aforesaid amount within two months from the date of this order.

After deposit of compensation amount 25% of the amount shall be kept in FD in the name of petitioner in any Nationalized or Scheduled Bank of his choice for a period of 2 years and balance 75% shall be disbursed to the petitioner through E-payment on proper identification.

Taking into account the medical evidence and the overall circumstances, this Tribunal reasonably assesses the functional disability at 10% to the whole body, which would meet the ends of justice.
